Cyber Attack Disrupts UK Electric Utilities, Operations Restored After Ransomware Incident

LONDON, June 17 — Several UK electric utility firms have resumed normal operations after a cyber attack last week disrupted internal IT systems and threatened electricity billing and customer service functions across parts of the country.

The incident, which began late on June 11, affected at least three regional energy providers, including Southland Power, Northshore Grids, and CityCurrent Electric, industry sources said. The attack, believed to be a ransomware infection, did not impact the delivery of electricity to homes or businesses, but hindered customer account access, billing processes, and some field service scheduling for several days.

Southland Power released a statement confirming that its core network infrastructure had been targeted, resulting in “temporary loss of access to customer portals and staff scheduling software.” The company said no customer payment or usage data had been compromised.

According to the UK Energy Networks Association, the utilities “acted swiftly to isolate affected systems and implement contingency plans,” working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) and private cybersecurity contractors.

“Thanks to robust response protocols, electricity supply itself was never under threat,” said Genevieve Carter, a spokesperson for the Association. “But the attack underlines the growing cyber risks facing critical infrastructure.”

All three affected companies reported that normal account access and billing services were fully restored by Sunday evening. An NCSC spokesperson said the incident was resolved without payment to the attackers. “Our teams supported the utilities in containing the ransomware, analysing the breach, and ensuring safe restoration of services,” the spokesperson said.

The GMB union, which represents many utility workers, praised staff for their “rapid response in difficult circumstances,” noting that manual workarounds had been deployed to keep essential services running.

Industry analysts estimate that the disruption affected more than 1.2 million customer accounts across the three companies, though no outages occurred. “This was a wake-up call,” said Fiona Marsh, a utilities sector analyst at Pinnacle Advisory. “While the grid itself remained secure, digital systems are now an essential part of the sector’s resilience.”

Authorities have launched a criminal investigation and said they are monitoring for further threats. The NCSC urged all utilities to review cybersecurity measures and patch known vulnerabilities.
